analogy.p: Think of the population as a whole cake and a sample as a spoonful. If you take a spoonful from a well mixed cake, you can taste the spoon and judge the whole cake; that is a random sample. If you only scoop the icing off the top, you taste something unrepresentative: that is bias. A stratified spoonful would be like taking a bit from every layer in proportion to its thickness. A pie chart is like cutting that cake into slices, where the angle of each slice shows its share. The analogy breaks down because a real population is made of individuals who can differ in many ways at once, so random selection is much harder to guarantee than stirring a cake.

bullets: **Pie chart**: a circle divided into sectors whose angles are proportional to the frequencies.
**Stem and leaf diagram**: a way of listing every data value in order, grouped by their first digit(s), so you keep the raw data while seeing the shape.
**Sampling**: choosing part of a **population** so that conclusions about the sample can be applied to the whole population.
**Stratified sampling** (Higher): sample sizes in each group are proportional to the size of the group in the population.
Typical tasks: draw a pie chart with a protractor, find a frequency from an angle, read a median or quartile from a stem and leaf, calculate stratified sample sizes, and comment on bias.
You must always show working: the angle calculation, the key, the fraction used for the sample.
core.h: What this spec point asks you to do
core.p: This point brings together three skills from the Statistics section of Edexcel GCSE Maths Higher (1MA1): **constructing and interpreting pie charts**, **constructing and interpreting stem and leaf diagrams**, and **sampling** (using a sample to infer things about a population, understanding why the sample must be random, and using **stratified sampling** at Higher tier). All three are about turning raw data into something you can read quickly and about knowing how far a conclusion can be trusted. They appear on Paper 1, 2 and 3, usually worth 2 to 5 marks each, and sampling questions often ask you to explain or comment, not just calculate.

bullets: The full circle = 360 degrees = the **total frequency**.
Sector angle is proportional to frequency: bigger angle means more items.
Used for **categorical** (or discrete) data such as favourite sport, type of transport, eye colour.
Good for comparing each category with the whole (for example 'about a quarter walk').
Poor for reading exact values or for many tiny categories.
A sector of 90 degrees is one quarter; 180 degrees is one half; 120 degrees is one third; 60 degrees is one sixth.
Every sector should be labelled with the category (and often the angle or frequency), and the chart should have a title.
core.h: Pie charts: what they show and when they are used
core.p: A **pie chart** shows how a total is shared between categories. The whole circle (360 degrees) represents **all** the data, and each **sector** represents one category. The angle of a sector is **proportional to its frequency**, so a sector with twice the angle has twice the frequency. Pie charts are best for showing proportions or fractions of a whole for **categorical data** with a small number of categories. Their weakness is that you cannot read exact frequencies from them unless you know the total.

bullets: Step 1: add the frequencies to find the **total**.
Step 2: calculate degrees per item = **360 / total**.
Step 3: angle for each category = **frequency x (360 / total)**, or equivalently (frequency / total) x 360.
Step 4: **check** the angles add up to 360 degrees.
Step 5: draw a circle, draw a radius, and measure the first angle with a protractor (centre of protractor on the centre of the circle, zero line along the radius).
Step 6: from the end of that line, measure the next angle, and so on. The last sector should close automatically; if it does not, check your angles.
Step 7: label each sector (and the angle or frequency) and give the chart a title.
Example: total 60, so 360 / 60 = 6 degrees per item; 18 walkers gives 18 x 6 = 108 degrees.
core.h: Drawing a pie chart step by step
core.p: To draw a pie chart you must turn each frequency into an angle. The key idea is that the total frequency shares out the 360 degrees, so **one item is worth 360 divided by the total**. Work out that 'degrees per item' first, multiply it by each frequency, and then check that all angles add up to 360. Then draw the circle with compasses and use a protractor to measure each angle from a radius, going round in order. Marks are given for correct angles (usually allowing a tolerance of about 2 degrees), for labels, and for the sectors adding to a full circle.

bullets: Frequency of a sector = **(angle / 360) x total frequency**.
Fraction of the whole = **angle / 360** (simplify, for example 90/360 = 1/4).
Percentage of the whole = **(angle / 360) x 100**.
If you know the frequency and angle of one sector, you can find the total: **total = frequency x 360 / angle**.
To compare two pie charts you must compare **proportions** (angles) and be careful about differing totals.
Statements such as 'more people chose bus in chart B' are not valid from angles alone if the totals differ; say 'a greater **proportion**'.
The largest sector is the **modal category** (the mode) because it has the highest frequency.
core.p: When you read a pie chart you use the angle as a **fraction of 360**. If the total frequency is known, the frequency of a sector is (angle / 360) x total. If the total is not given, you can only talk about **proportions or fractions**, not actual numbers. This is the single most important idea for comparing two pie charts: **equal angles do not mean equal frequencies unless the totals are equal.** A 90 degree sector in a chart of 40 people is 10 people, but a 90 degree sector in a chart of 200 people is 50 people.

bullets: From one sector: if 20 people have angle 75 degrees, then 1 degree = 20 / 75 people, so total = 360 x 20 / 75 = 96.
Use ratio ideas: angles are in the same ratio as the frequencies.
If angles are given algebraically (for example x, 2x, 3x and 90), form the equation x + 2x + 3x + 90 = 360, then solve.
Remaining angle = 360 minus the sum of the angles already known.
Convert angles to fractions (for example 54/360 = 3/20) to find expected counts in probability or estimate questions.
Check: do your frequencies add to the total, and do your angles add to 360?
Never read a frequency off the chart by eye; always calculate it.
core.p: Higher tier questions often give you part of the information and ask you to work backwards. A common one gives the angle and frequency for one sector, so you find the value for **one degree** or **one item**, then scale to get the total or other sectors. Another gives the total and says that two sectors are equal or that one angle is a multiple of another, so you must form and solve an equation using the fact that all angles sum to 360. Writing a clear unit rate ('1 person = 6 degrees') keeps the working organised and earns method marks even if you slip on arithmetic.

bullets: Step 1: decide the stems (for two digit numbers the tens digits; for numbers like 3.4 the whole numbers).
Step 2: go through the data and write each leaf next to its stem **in the order given** (an unordered draft).
Step 3: **redraw with the leaves in order**, smallest to largest, and **evenly spaced** in columns.
Step 4: add a **key**, for example 'Key: 2 | 3 means 23 minutes' (always include units).
Include a stem even if it has no leaves (for example a gap between 30s and 50s), so the shape is not distorted.
Repeated values are written repeatedly: two 23s give 2 | 3 3.
If the data has decimals, the key must make the decimal place clear: 'Key: 4 | 7 means 4.7 kg'.
Keep leaves equally spaced so the lengths of rows can be compared visually.
core.p: A **stem and leaf diagram** shows every individual data value, split into a **stem** (the leading digit or digits) and a **leaf** (the final digit). The leaves are written in rows next to their stem, and the diagram looks like a sideways bar chart, so you can see the **shape** of the distribution and still read every actual value. It is only used for **numerical** data. The values must be ordered in the final version, and the diagram must have a **key** that shows how to read it, for example 2 | 3 means 23.

bullets: **n** = total number of leaves; count them carefully, row by row.
**Median** position = (n + 1) / 2. If this is not a whole number, the median is halfway between the two middle values.
**Lower quartile (Q1)** position = (n + 1) / 4; **upper quartile (Q3)** position = 3(n + 1) / 4.
**Range** = largest value - smallest value.
**Mode** = the value that appears most; look for repeated leaves in one row.
Reading from the key, convert back to real values: stem 4 leaf 7 with key 4 | 7 = 47.
The row with the longest line of leaves shows the **modal class** (the group with the most data).
Shape: leaves bunched at low stems means a positive skew; symmetrical means roughly balanced.
core.h: Reading a stem and leaf diagram
core.p: Because every value is shown, you can read off statistics exactly. The **mode** is the most common value (the leaf that repeats most in a row), the **range** is the largest value minus the smallest, and the **median** is the middle value, found by counting in from either end. The count of leaves gives the sample size n. For quartiles you use the position rules: **lower quartile at (n + 1)/4**, **median at (n + 1)/2**, and **upper quartile at 3(n + 1)/4**, then **interquartile range = upper quartile - lower quartile**. Always give the actual value, not just the position.

bullets: The stem is in the **middle**; leaves on both sides are written in increasing order moving **away** from the stem.
Two keys are needed, for example 'Girls: 3 | 2 means 23' and 'Boys: 2 | 3 means 23'.
To compare, calculate a median (or mean) for each side, and a range or IQR for each side.
Always put the comparison in context: 'The median for the girls is higher than for the boys, so on average the girls took longer.'
Comment on both an average and the spread: a smaller range or IQR means the data is **more consistent**.
Check the number of leaves on each side separately because n may differ.
Do not mix the two sets when finding the median; each side is its own data set.
core.p: A **back-to-back stem and leaf diagram** compares two data sets using one central stem. One set's leaves run to the left and the other's run to the right. The leaves on the **left** side are read in order from the stem outward, which means the smallest leaf is closest to the stem and bigger leaves are further left. It is a very efficient way to compare two groups, and the exam question almost always asks you to compare an **average** and a **spread**. You need two keys, one for each side.

bullets: **Population**: every member of the group being studied.
**Sample**: a subset of the population chosen to represent it.
**Census**: data collected from the whole population.
Reasons for sampling: cheaper, quicker, practical, and necessary when testing is destructive (for example crash tests, bulb lifetimes).
Advantage of a census: no sampling error, completely accurate. Disadvantage: expensive and time consuming.
Sample results are **estimates**: another sample would give slightly different results.
The aim is that the sample is **representative** of the population: it has the same mix of characteristics.
core.p: The **population** is the whole group you want to know about (for example every student in a school, every battery produced by a factory). A **census** collects data from **every member** of the population, which gives the exact answer but is usually too slow, too costly, or impossible (for example if testing destroys the item, such as testing how long a battery lasts). A **sample** is a smaller selection taken from the population. We use data from the sample to **make inferences** about the population, knowing the answer will be an **estimate** and not an exact value.

bullets: **Random sample**: every member has an **equal chance** of selection, and selections are independent of any characteristic of interest.
**Bias**: results are unfairly weighted towards one group; this makes the sample unrepresentative.
Examples of biased samples: asking only your friends, surveying at a single location or time, volunteer responses, asking the first 10 people in a queue.
Method for a simple random sample: number every member of the population, then generate random numbers (calculator or computer) and select those members.
A **larger sample** is generally more reliable than a smaller one because random variation matters less.
A bigger sample does not fix bias: a large biased sample is still biased.
Comment in context: 'The sample is biased because it only includes students in Year 7, who may not represent the whole school.'
core.p: A good sample must be **random**, which means **every member of the population has an equal chance of being chosen**. Random selection prevents **bias**, which is a systematic tendency for the sample to favour some members of the population over others. If you survey only people at a gym about how much exercise people do, or only students in one class about the whole school, the results will be biased. Random methods include numbering all members and using a random number generator or drawing numbers from a hat. A sample chosen for convenience, or one where people volunteer, is likely to be biased.

bullets: **Number from a stratum** = (size of stratum / size of population) x total sample size.
Equivalent method: find the sampling fraction = sample size / population size, then multiply each stratum by it.
Within each stratum, choose the individuals at random.
Round to whole people if needed; check the total still equals the sample size, adjusting sensibly.
Example: population 900, sample 60, so sampling fraction 60/900 = 1/15. A stratum of 360 gives 360/15 = 24.
Stratified sampling is used when the population has distinct groups with different characteristics.
It is more representative than a simple random sample of the same size because it guarantees every group is represented in proportion.
Show the fraction, the multiplication and the final whole number for full marks.
core.p: In **stratified sampling** the population is split into groups called **strata** (for example year groups, age bands or genders), and a random sample is taken from each stratum so that the sample has **the same proportions as the population**. This makes the sample representative of each subgroup, which matters when the groups are likely to give different answers. The number to take from each stratum is found with a simple proportion calculation. Always check that the numbers sampled add up to the total sample size.

bullets: Estimate for population = **(proportion in sample) x (population size)**.
Reliability improves with a **larger** sample, **random** selection, and no bias.
Taking **repeated samples** and averaging them also improves reliability.
Say 'estimate', 'approximately' or 'expected' to show you know it is not exact.
Limitations: small samples vary a lot; sampling methods may be biased; people may not answer honestly; the sample may miss a rare group.
Questions may ask 'Is the sample suitable?': check size, randomness and whether it includes everyone relevant.
A statement about the sample should not be turned into a certain statement about the population.
core.p: After sampling, you use the sample to **estimate** a population value. For example, if 15 of a random sample of 60 students cycle to school, the estimate for a school of 900 is 15/60 x 900 = 225 students. The estimate is more **reliable** when the sample is **random**, **large enough**, and **representative** (for example stratified when groups differ). It is never certain. Examiners reward comments that say the result is an estimate, that a different sample could give a different answer, and that a bigger sample or repeating the sampling would improve reliability.

bullets: Pie chart: proportions of categories; stem and leaf: all values for a small data set; both lose different information.
A stem and leaf diagram gives mean, median, mode and range directly; a pie chart only gives the modal category and proportions.
Relative frequency from a sample = estimated probability, which links to Probability.
Angles in a pie chart link to angles at a point (sum 360 degrees).
Sampling fractions use ratio and proportion; the same method as sharing in a ratio.
Capture-recapture is another way to estimate a population, built on the same sampling ideas (see the Capture-recapture point).
Interpreting charts with percentages links to percentage change and reverse percentage skills.
core.h: Choosing the right diagram and links to other topics
core.p: Knowing which diagram to use is part of the skill. Pie charts display proportions of a whole for categorical data, stem and leaf diagrams display the individual values of a small numerical data set, bar charts compare frequencies, and histograms or cumulative frequency graphs handle large or grouped continuous data. These ideas connect to averages (mean, median, mode from raw data), to **probability** (relative frequency from a sample estimates probability), to **fractions, percentages and ratio** (angles and sampling fractions), and to **algebra** (forming equations for unknown angles).

exam: **Command words**: 'Draw' a pie chart means use a protractor and label sectors; 'Work out' means show calculation; 'Explain' or 'Comment' needs a reason in context.
Pie chart drawing is usually 3 to 4 marks: 1 mark for the method (360 / total), 1 for the correct angles, 1 for accuracy within tolerance and 1 for labelling. Show 360 / total on the paper.
For 'find the frequency from the angle' (2 marks): write (angle / 360) x total, then the answer. State the unit or category.
For comparing two pie charts (2 marks): use the word '**proportion**' and refer to both charts, for example 'A greater proportion of group A chose walking.'
Stem and leaf diagrams: marks for correct stems, for leaves in order, for equal spacing and for the **key**. Always write the key even if not asked.
For median/quartiles from a stem and leaf: count n, write the position, then state the value. A typical 3 mark question gives method marks for positions.
Interquartile range = upper quartile - lower quartile; spread comparisons (2 marks) should say 'smaller IQR means more consistent'.
Comparison questions (back-to-back): one comment on average, one on spread, both **in context** with figures, typically 2 to 4 marks.
Sampling 'Give a reason' questions (1 mark): 'it is biased because...', 'sample too small', 'only includes one group', always in context.
Stratified sampling (2 to 3 marks): show stratum / population x sample size for each stratum and check the total; unrounded values should be sensible whole numbers.
'Explain how to take a random sample' (2 marks): number every member, use a random number generator, choose the required number of members from the numbers generated.
6 mark style: do not just describe; link the data collected, the diagram used, the calculation and a final conclusion, and say what the limitation is.

mistakes.r: Calculate: frequency = (angle / 360) x total. Show the working.
mistakes.w: Reading a frequency from a pie chart sector by comparing sizes by eye.

mistakes.r: Compare **proportions** or fractions, not frequencies, unless the totals are known and equal.
mistakes.w: Saying 'more people chose bus in chart B' because the sector is bigger, when the two charts have different totals.

mistakes.r: Always check the total of the angles is 360 before drawing; recheck degrees per item (360 / total).
mistakes.w: Angles in a pie chart that do not add up to 360 degrees.

mistakes.r: Add all frequencies to get the total, then 360 divided by that total.
mistakes.w: Using the wrong total, for example dividing 360 by the largest frequency.

mistakes.r: Always include a key such as '2 | 3 means 23 minutes'. The key earns a mark.
mistakes.w: Forgetting the key on a stem and leaf diagram, or writing a key without units.

mistakes.r: Redraw so leaves are in increasing order from the stem and equally spaced.
mistakes.w: Leaves not in order or unevenly spaced in the final stem and leaf diagram.

mistakes.r: Count the leaves to find n, then use (n + 1)/2 to find the position and count along in order.
mistakes.w: Finding the median of a stem and leaf diagram by picking the middle row rather than the middle value.

mistakes.r: Include every stem from lowest to highest, even if it has no leaves.
mistakes.w: Leaving out an empty stem so the diagram looks continuous.

mistakes.r: Random means every member has an equal chance of selection; size affects reliability, randomness affects bias.
mistakes.w: Describing a sample as random just because it is big, or biased only because it is small.

mistakes.r: Use (stratum / population) x sample size, and check the numbers add to the total sample size.
mistakes.w: Stratified sample: using sample size divided by stratum size, or rounding so the total no longer matches.

summary: You must construct and interpret pie charts (angle = frequency / total x 360), construct and read ordered stem and leaf diagrams including back-to-back ones, and understand sampling: populations, random samples, bias and, at Higher tier, stratified sampling. It matters because these skills let you present and trust data, and sampling questions test your reasoning about reliability as much as your calculations.

terms.d: A circular chart divided into sectors, where the angle of each sector is proportional to the frequency of that category.
One slice of a pie chart; its angle represents the frequency of one category.
360 divided by the total frequency; the angle that represents a single data item in a pie chart.
Data that is sorted into named groups or categories rather than measured numerically.
A diagram that shows all the data values by splitting each into a stem (leading digit or digits) and a leaf (final digit).
The leading digit(s) of a data value in a stem and leaf diagram, written in a column.
The final digit of a data value in a stem and leaf diagram, written in order along the row of its stem.
A statement that explains how to read a stem and leaf diagram, for example 2 | 3 means 23 minutes.
A stem and leaf diagram with a shared central stem and leaves on both sides, used to compare two data sets.
The whole group of people or items that you want to find out about.
A selection from the population, used to find out about the population.
A survey of every member of the population.
A sample in which every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected.
A systematic error that makes a sample unrepresentative by favouring some members of the population over others.
A sample in which the population is divided into groups (strata) and the number sampled from each group is proportional to the size of that group.
One of the groups into which a population is divided for stratified sampling.
The sample size divided by the population size.
A conclusion about a population drawn from the results of a sample.
A sample that has the same characteristics, in the same proportions, as the population.

worked.ans: (a) Walk 108 degrees, Bus 144 degrees, Car 54 degrees, Cycle 54 degrees. (b) 96 people.
worked.q: 60 students were asked how they travel to school: Walk 18, Bus 24, Car 9, Cycle 9. (a) Work out the angle for each category in a pie chart. (b) In a second pie chart, a sector of 75 degrees represents 20 people. Work out the total number of people in the second chart. [5 marks]
steps: Walk: 18 x 6 = 108 degrees. Bus: 24 x 6 = 144 degrees. Car: 9 x 6 = 54 degrees. Cycle: 9 x 6 = 54 degrees.
(b) 75 degrees represents 20 people, so total people = 360 / 75 x 20 = 4.8 x 20 = 96.

worked.ans: Median 30 years, IQR 20 years, range 40 years, with the diagram drawn in order and the key given.
worked.q: The ages of 15 people are: 23, 31, 15, 41, 26, 34, 12, 38, 21, 47, 30, 23, 52, 17, 45. (a) Draw an ordered stem and leaf diagram with a key. (b) Find the median, the interquartile range and the range. [6 marks]
steps: (a) Stems 1 to 5. Leaves in order: 1 | 2 5 7; 2 | 1 3 3 6; 3 | 0 1 4 8; 4 | 1 5 7; 5 | 2. Key: 2 | 3 means 23 years.
Lower quartile position = (15 + 1) / 4 = 4th value = 21. Upper quartile position = 3 x 16 / 4 = 12th value = 41.

worked.ans: (a) Year 9: 24, Year 10: 21, Year 11: 15. (b) The stratified sample is representative of all year groups, so there is no bias from leaving out groups.
worked.q: A school has 900 students: Year 9 has 360, Year 10 has 315 and Year 11 has 225. A stratified sample of 60 students is taken. (a) Work out the number from each year group. (b) Give one reason why a stratified sample is better than asking 60 students from Year 9 only. [4 marks]
steps: (b) Asking only Year 9 is biased because it leaves out Years 10 and 11, whose answers might differ. A stratified sample represents each year group in proportion to its size.
